title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Renal regulation. Kidneys excrete H⁺ (phosphate, ammonium) and reabsorb or regenerate HCO₃⁻.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respiratory regulation. The open bicarbonate buffer lets the lungs change PCO₂ quickly.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic acidosis. Loss of bicarbonate or gain of acid; lungs compensate by hyperventilating (lower PCO₂).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic alkalosis. Excess bicarbonate or loss of acid (vomiting); lungs hypoventilate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respiratory acidosis. CO₂ retention lowers pH; kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respiratory alkalosis. Excess CO₂ elimination raises pH; kidneys excrete bicarbonate.

title: Normal pH values?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Normal pH values?
body.back: Arterial 7.38-7.42; venous 7.36-7.41; compatible with life ~7.00-7.80.

title: Acid, base, strong vs weak?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Acid, base, strong vs weak?
body.back: Acid releases H⁺, base captures H⁺; strong acid: high Ka, low pKa; weak acid: low Ka, high pKa.

title: Bicarbonate buffer values?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Bicarbonate buffer values?
body.back: pKa 6.1; HCO₃⁻ 24-28 mmol/L; PCO₂ 40 ± 3 mmHg; CO₂ solubility 0.03 mmol/L/mmHg.

title: Henderson-Hasselbalch for blood?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Henderson-Hasselbalch for blood?
body.back: pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PCO₂); normal ratio 20:1 → pH 7.40.

title: Closed buffers?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Closed buffers?
body.back: Phosphate (pKa 6.82; intracellular and renal), proteins, haemoglobin (main red-cell buffer).

title: Four acid-base disorders?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Four acid-base disorders?
body.back: Respiratory acidosis (PCO₂ ↑), respiratory alkalosis (PCO₂ ↓), metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ ↓), metabolic alkalosis (HCO₃⁻ ↑).

title: Compensation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Compensation?
body.back: Lungs change PCO₂ in minutes; kidneys adjust H⁺ excretion and HCO₃⁻ over hours to days.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bernoulli's theorem. Energy conservation: in a stenosis velocity rises and pressure falls; in an aneurysm the reverse.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Continuity. Q = S·v: total cross-section is maximal in capillaries, so velocity is lowest there.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Laplace's law. Wall tension rises with pressure and radius: dilated vessels and aneurysms are under more tension.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Poiseuille's law. Laminar flow is proportional to r⁴ and ΔP, inversely to viscosity and length; high viscosity raises resistance.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reynolds number. High in the aorta (≈ 4,500): turbulent flow; low in medium vessels: laminar.

title: Components and aims of the circulation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Components and aims of the circulation?
body.back: Pump (heart), fluid (blood), closed conduits (vessels); deliver O₂ and nutrients, remove waste, adapted to needs.

title: Pulmonary vs systemic circuits?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Pulmonary vs systemic circuits?
body.back: Right heart → pulmonary artery → lungs; left heart → aorta → organs.

title: Poiseuille's law and its consequence?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Poiseuille's law and its consequence?
body.back: Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL); raised viscosity lowers flow, so pressure rises (hypertension).

title: Flow regimes in vessels?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Flow regimes in vessels?
body.back: Large vessels turbulent (aorta R ≈ 4,500); medium laminar; capillaries single-file red cells.

title: Bernoulli in stenosis and aneurysm?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Bernoulli in stenosis and aneurysm?
body.back: Stenosis: v ↑, P ↓, murmur and thrill. Aneurysm: v ↓, P ↑.

title: Velocity along the vascular tree?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Velocity along the vascular tree?
body.back: Falls from aorta to capillaries (max total section), rises again in veins.

title: Laplace's law?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Laplace's law?
body.back: T = P·r: wall tension increases with pressure and radius.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple convection. Solvent and solutes pushed together by a hydrostatic pressure difference.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple diffusion. Molecules move from high to low concentration or partial pressure (Fick's law).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Donnan equilibrium. Non-diffusible macro-ions (proteins) cause an unequal distribution of small ions and a membrane potential.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrochemical migration. Ions respond to combined chemical and electrical gradients.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrical migration. Ions move under an electric potential difference; cations and anions in opposite directions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Equilibrium potential. When only one ion can cross, charge separation builds a potential that stops net flow: E = (RT/zF) ln(C₁/C₂).

title: Membrane characteristics?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Membrane characteristics?
body.back: Thickness d, particle mobility u, diffusion coefficient D = RTu, permeability P = D/d.

title: Types of membranes?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Types of membranes?
body.back: Semipermeable (solvent only), dialysis (not macromolecules), selective (some ions/molecules).

title: Passive vs active transport?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Passive vs active transport?
body.back: Passive: no energy, down a gradient (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis). Active: ATP, against a gradient.

title: Four elementary passive phenomena?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Four elementary passive phenomena?
body.back: Simple diffusion (concentration), convection (pressure), electrical migration (potential), electrochemical migration.

title: Equilibrium (Nernst) potential?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Equilibrium (Nernst) potential?
body.back: One permeant ion diffuses, charge separates until the potential balances the gradient: E = (RT/zF) ln(C₁/C₂).

title: Donnan equilibrium vs diffusion potential?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Donnan equilibrium vs diffusion potential?
body.back: Donnan: impermeant macro-ions cause unequal small-ion distribution. Diffusion potential: ions crossing at different speeds.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chemical potential. Energy per mole related to concentration (or partial pressure): µ = µ⁰ + RT ln C.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrochemical potential. Chemical plus electrical terms for ions: governs ion movement across membranes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrical potential. Energy per unit charge: ΔE = q(V_A − V_B), in volts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gravitational potential. Potential energy mgh per unit mass: g·h, in J/kg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fundamental property. A spontaneous displacement lowers potential energy; moving uphill needs external energy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Work and energy. W = −ΔE; for a fluid, dW = P·dV.

title: Define work and its sign.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define work and its sign.
body.back: dW = F·dl·cos α (J); positive for α < 90°, negative for α > 90°, zero at 90°.

title: Work for a fluid?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Work for a fluid?
body.back: dW = P·dV.

title: Relationship between work and energy?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Relationship between work and energy?
body.back: W = −ΔE: positive work is spontaneous (energy lost); negative work requires external energy.

title: Potential energy vs potential?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Potential energy vs potential?
body.back: Potential energy difference ΔE = −W depends on the amount; potential difference ΔY = ΔE/X is per unit quantity.

title: Fundamental property of potentials?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Fundamental property of potentials?
body.back: Spontaneous movement goes from high to low potential (energy decreases); going up requires external energy.

title: Main potentials?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Main potentials?
body.back: Gravitational gh (J/kg), electrical V (J/C), chemical µ = µ⁰ + RT ln C, electrochemical µ̃ = µ + zFV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Arterial segment. 35 − 6 + 6 − 28 = +7 mmHg: water and small solutes leave the blood (nutritive effect).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Interstitial compartment. Low hydrostatic (≈ 6 mmHg) and oncotic (≈ 6 mmHg) pressures.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Starling equation. Net flow set by hydrostatic minus oncotic pressure differences across a dialysis-like membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Venous segment. 20 − 6 + 6 − 28 = −8 mmHg: water returns to the blood, carrying metabolic waste.

title: Distribution of body water?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Distribution of body water?
body.back: Intracellular ≈ 40% (28 L); extracellular ≈ 20-21%: interstitial ≈ 15% (10-11 L), plasma ≈ 4% (3 L), lymph 1-2%.

title: Starling equation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Starling equation?
body.back: Φ₁→₂ = K·S·(P₁ − P₂ − π₁ + π₂): hydrostatic minus oncotic pressure differences.

title: Intestinal absorption of water?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Intestinal absorption of water?
body.back: Between meals: 2 − 20 − 0 + 28 = +10 (absorption); digestion: +108; congestion (capillary P > 30): reversal, diarrhoea.

title: Capillary exchange values?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Capillary exchange values?
body.back: Arterial end: 35 − 6 + 6 − 28 = +7 (filtration). Venous end: 20 − 6 + 6 − 28 = −8 (reabsorption).

title: Causes of oedema by Starling forces?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Causes of oedema by Starling forces?
body.back: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous congestion) or lowered plasma oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Boyle-Mariotte's law. At constant n and T, volume falls as pressure rises: PV is constant.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Charles's law. At constant n and P, volume varies linearly with absolute temperature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Partial pressures. Each gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times total pressure; the total is their sum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gay-Lussac's law. At constant n and V, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ideal gas equation. PV = nRT (SI units); 1 mol occupies 22.4 L at 0 °C and 1 atm.

title: Units of pressure?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Units of pressure?
body.back: Pa = N/m²; 1 mmHg = 133.3 Pa; 1 atm = 760 mmHg ≈ 101 kPa ≈ 10 m water ≈ 1 bar.

title: Fundamental law of fluid statics?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Fundamental law of fluid statics?
body.back: In a fluid at rest, pressure is equal in all directions, equal on a horizontal plane, and increases linearly with depth (ΔP = ρgh).

title: Transmural pressure?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Transmural pressure?
body.back: Inside − outside pressure of a vessel or alveolus: positive distends, zero/negative allows collapse.

title: Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac laws?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac laws?
body.back: Boyle: PV constant (n, T). Charles: V ∝ T (n, P). Gay-Lussac: P ∝ T (n, V).

title: Ideal gas equation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Ideal gas equation?
body.back: PV = nRT; R = 8.314 J/mol·K; 1 mol = 22.4 L at 0 °C, 1 atm.

title: STPD, BTPS, ATPS?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: STPD, BTPS, ATPS?
body.back: STPD: 0 °C, 1 atm, dry. BTPS: 37 °C, ambient P, saturated. ATPS: ambient T and P, saturated.

title: Mole fraction and partial pressure?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Mole fraction and partial pressure?
body.back: xᵢ = nᵢ/n; Pᵢ = xᵢ·P; Dalton: total P = Σ Pᵢ.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Centrifugation. Rotation creates an acceleration ω²R much larger than g, separating cells, bacteria, macromolecules.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diffusion. Internal cause: particles move down their concentration gradient.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Stokes' law. Viscous drag opposes motion, proportional to viscosity and velocity; for a sphere R = −6πrηv; velocity quickly becomes constant.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electrophoresis. Charged macro-ions move at speeds set by charge, size and shape, separating proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sedimentation. Apparent weight (weight − Archimedes' thrust) drives particles down: red cells settle in anticoagulated blood (ESR).

title: Define migration movement.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define migration movement.
body.back: Movement of some particles while others (the solvent) remain stationary.

title: Stokes' law?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Stokes' law?
body.back: Drag R = −kηv; for a sphere R = −6πrηv; velocity becomes constant when drag balances the driving force.

title: Driving force in sedimentation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Driving force in sedimentation?
body.back: Apparent weight: V·g(ρ_s − ρ₀).

title: What is the ESR?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is the ESR?
body.back: Height of red-cell-free plasma after 1 hour in anticoagulated blood; normal < 10 mm; raised in infection or inflammation.

title: Centrifugation principle?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Centrifugation principle?
body.back: Rotation gives γ = ω²R ≫ g to separate cells, bacteria, macromolecules.

title: Migration in an electric field?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Migration in an electric field?
body.back: F = qE; v = uE (u = mobility); flux Φ = C·S·v.

title: Principle of electrophoresis?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Principle of electrophoresis?
body.back: Macro-ions move at different speeds in a field and separate (e.g. serum proteins).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Concentrated compartment. Water enters, tending to equalise concentrations.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dilute compartment. Water has the higher chemical potential here and flows out.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Semipermeable membrane. Passes water but not the solute.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oncotic pressure. Osmotic pressure of plasma proteins, pulling water into capillaries and keeping blood volume stable.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Van't Hoff's law. Osmotic pressure proportional to osmolarity of non-diffusible particles and absolute temperature.

title: Define osmosis.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define osmosis.
body.back: Flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution, driven by the solvent's chemical potential.

title: Define osmotic pressure.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define osmotic pressure.
body.back: The minimum pressure applied to the concentrated side to prevent solvent passage.

title: Van't Hoff's law?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Van't Hoff's law?
body.back: ω = RTC, with C = osmolarity of non-diffusible particles, T in kelvin, R = 8.31 J/mol·K.

title: Macromolecules and osmotic pressure?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Macromolecules and osmotic pressure?
body.back: ω = RTC + RTvC²: excluded volume makes it slightly higher than Van't Hoff.

title: Donnan effect?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Donnan effect?
body.back: Non-diffusible macro-ions cause unequal diffusible-ion concentrations, a Donnan potential and extra Donnan pressure.

title: Plasma oncotic pressure?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Plasma oncotic pressure?
body.back: ≈ 28 mmHg (3.2 kPa) at 37 °C, ~85% from albumin; keeps water in capillaries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alveolar air. PO₂ ≈ 100-103, PCO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Atmospheric air. PO₂ ≈ 152 mmHg, PCO₂ ≈ 0.2 mmHg at sea level.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pulmonary capillary (entering). Venous blood PO₂ ≈ 40, PCO₂ ≈ 47 mmHg: O₂ enters the blood, CO₂ leaves.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alveolar-capillary diffusion. Flux proportional to diffusion coefficient, solubility, surface and pressure difference, inversely to membrane thickness.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tissue exchange. In tissues the gradients reverse: O₂ diffuses to cells, CO₂ to blood.

title: Five processes of respiration?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Five processes of respiration?
body.back: Pulmonary ventilation, gas exchange in lungs, gas transport in blood, gas exchange in tissues, mitochondrial oxidation.

title: Zones of the respiratory system?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Zones of the respiratory system?
body.back: Conduction zone (to terminal bronchioles: warm, filter, humidify) and respiratory zone (lobules, alveoli: exchange).

title: Partial pressures along the path?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Partial pressures along the path?
body.back: Atmosphere PO₂ 152, PCO₂ 0.2; alveolus PO₂ ~100, PCO₂ 40; venous blood PO₂ 40, PCO₂ 47 mmHg.

title: Fick's law for alveolar diffusion?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Fick's law for alveolar diffusion?
body.back: Flux ∝ diffusion coefficient × solubility × surface × ΔP / membrane thickness; CO₂ ~20× more soluble than O₂.

title: Role of surfactant?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Role of surfactant?
body.back: Made by type II pneumocytes; lowers surface tension, prevents end-expiratory collapse (Laplace), opens newborn lungs; absence → hyaline membrane disease.

title: Transport of O₂ and CO₂?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Transport of O₂ and CO₂?
body.back: O₂: ~98% on haemoglobin, rest dissolved. CO₂: ~70% bicarbonate, ~20% carbamino, ~7-10% dissolved.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coulomb force. Attraction between ions, inversely proportional to the dielectric constant and distance squared; water's high ε (78.5) separates ions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gas. Very low density; shape and volume set by the container; compressible and expandable.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Liquid. Close but disordered molecules; takes the container's shape; nearly incompressible.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dispersing causes. Electron-cloud repulsion at contact (Pauli) and Brownian thermal agitation, rising with temperature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Solid. Strong interactions, dense, definite shape and volume.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Solvation. Ions attract the opposite poles of solvent dipoles; in water, hydration (Na⁺ surrounded by water oxygens).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Van der Waals forces. Attraction between neutral molecules behaving as dipoles; very short range.

title: What determines the state of matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What determines the state of matter?
body.back: Competition between attractive forces (Coulomb, Van der Waals, ion-dipole) and dispersing causes (repulsion, thermal agitation).

title: Coulomb's law and water?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Coulomb's law and water?
body.back: F = kqq′/(εd²); water's high ε (78.5) weakens ionic attraction → electrolytic dissociation.

title: Van der Waals and solvation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Van der Waals and solvation?
body.back: Van der Waals: attraction between dipoles of neutral molecules. Solvation: ions surrounded by solvent dipoles (hydration in water).

title: Properties of solid, liquid, gas, gel?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Properties of solid, liquid, gas, gel?
body.back: Solid: ordered, fixed shape and volume. Liquid: fixed volume, flows. Gas: compressible. Gel: macromolecular network enclosing a liquid.

title: Melting and supercooling?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Melting and supercooling?
body.back: Melting occurs at constant temperature; a liquid can supercool below its freezing point before solidifying.

title: Cryoscopy?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Cryoscopy?
body.back: Δθ = K × osmolality (K = 1.86 for water); used to measure osmolality of plasma (≈ −0.56 °C).

title: Role of evaporation in thermoregulation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Role of evaporation in thermoregulation?
body.back: Evaporating sweat absorbs latent heat, the main heat loss when ambient temperature is high.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electric current. Base dimension I; charge C = A·s.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Luminous intensity. Candela.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Length. Base dimension L; derived: area L², volume L³.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mass. Base dimension M; density M·L⁻³.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Amount of substance. Mole: Avogadro's number of entities.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Time. Base dimension T; velocity L·T⁻¹, acceleration L·T⁻².

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Temperature. Absolute temperature in kelvin.

title: Seven SI base quantities and units?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Seven SI base quantities and units?
body.back: Length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, luminous intensity cd.

title: Key derived units?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Key derived units?
body.back: N = kg·m·s⁻², Pa = N·m⁻², J, W = J·s⁻¹, Gy = J·kg⁻¹, Bq, C = A·s, V = J·C⁻¹.

title: Extensive vs intensive?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Extensive vs intensive?
body.back: Extensive: proportional to amount, additive (mass, volume). Intensive: independent of amount (temperature, pressure, concentration).

title: Purpose of a dimensional equation?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Purpose of a dimensional equation?
body.back: Express a quantity in base dimensions and check a formula's homogeneity (force M·L·T⁻²).

title: Systematic vs random error?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Systematic vs random error?
body.back: Systematic: constant bias, not reduced by repetition. Random: scatter, reduced by averaging.

title: Uncertainty propagation rules?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Uncertainty propagation rules?
body.back: Sums/differences: add absolute uncertainties. Products/quotients: add relative uncertainties.

title: Common SI prefixes?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Common SI prefixes?
body.back: kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹; milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹².

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Blood. Red cells behave as spheres (k = 2.6) and φ is the haematocrit: polycythaemia raises viscosity, anaemia lowers it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Einstein's law. Viscosity of a suspension rises with relative volume φ; k grows with particle asymmetry (> 1000 for linear molecules).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Newton's law of viscosity. Friction force between layers is proportional to area and velocity gradient.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plasma. Protein solution; linear macromolecules (fibrinogen, α2-globulin, dextrans) raise its viscosity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Units. SI pascal-second (formerly poiseuille); cgs poise; water ≈ 10⁻³ Pa·s at 20 °C.

title: Define viscosity.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define viscosity.
body.back: A fluid's resistance to flow, from friction between layers and intermolecular bonds.

title: Newton's law of viscosity and units?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Newton's law of viscosity and units?
body.back: F = η·S·dv/dx; η in Pa·s (1 Pa·s = 10 poise); dimension M·L⁻¹·T⁻¹.

title: Relative viscosity?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Relative viscosity?
body.back: η_r = η/η_water; unitless; water ≈ 10⁻³ Pa·s at 20 °C.

title: Factors affecting viscosity?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Factors affecting viscosity?
body.back: Fluid nature, temperature (↑T ↓η), solute concentration, particle shape and relative volume.

title: Einstein's law?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Einstein's law?
body.back: η = η°(1 + kφ); k = 2.6 for spheres, > 1000 for linear macromolecules.

title: Blood viscosity formula and variations?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Blood viscosity formula and variations?
body.back: η_blood = η_plasma(1 + 2.6 Ht); ↑ polycythaemia, cold, inflammation; ↓ anaemia.

title: Newtonian vs non-Newtonian?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Newtonian vs non-Newtonian?
body.back: Newtonian: η independent of velocity (water, plasma). Non-Newtonian: η changes with velocity (blood).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extracellular water. About 20% of body weight.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intracellular water. About 40% of body weight.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Interstitial fluid. About 15.5% of body weight, bathing the cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plasma water. About 4.5% of body weight.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Total body water. 60-65% of body weight, higher in infants (~75%), falling with age.

title: Body water distribution?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Body water distribution?
body.back: Total 60-65% (infant ~75%); intracellular ~40%; extracellular ~20% (interstitial ~15.5%, plasma ~4.5%).

title: Key physical properties of water?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Key physical properties of water?
body.back: Polar, hydrogen bonds; ice 0.91 g/cm³; specific heat 4.184 J/g·°C; surface tension ~72 mN/m; dielectric constant 78.5; amphoteric.

title: Define an equivalent.
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Define an equivalent.
body.back: The fraction of a mole of ions carrying one mole of charge (96,500 C); 1 mol of ion of valence z = z Eq.

title: Molarity vs molality; osmolarity vs osmolality?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Molarity vs molality; osmolarity vs osmolality?
body.back: Molarity: mol/L solution (sum = osmolarity). Molality: mol/kg solvent (sum = osmolality).

title: Equivalent concentration?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Equivalent concentration?
body.back: C_Eq = molarity × valence (Eq/L, mEq/L).

title: Principle of electroneutrality?
subject: subj:physics1

body.front: Principle of electroneutrality?
body.back: Σ anionic Eq = Σ cationic Eq in a solution; allows computing an unknown ion concentration.
